title: Three ceilings on the braking base
question: What independently limits the braking force?
scope: Schematic geometry is not measured; torque capability alone does not qualify a stopping bound.

steps.title: Brake through the floor
steps.description: Only the driven wheels supply the drawn retarding force. Their normal load and friction coefficient cap that force.

steps.title: Keep the body supported
steps.description: The inertial load acts at the center of gravity. Its height and the leading support distance constrain tipping independently of traction.

steps.title: Check the motor ceiling too
steps.description: Hub torque divided by wheel radius gives wheel force. The pair must supply the required force, but satisfying this ceiling does not establish floor friction or stability.

review_notes: Inspected rendered original artwork and local QMD context; original geometry retained.

title: Stopping distance of the warehouse mobile manipulator
question: Which stopping-distance term spends the remaining aisle clearance?
scope: These three computed cases use the chapter’s elementary stopping model; later profiles and tracking bounds are not included.

steps.title: Start with body-owned terms
steps.description: Case 1 separates blind travel, braking travel, and fixed overhead. Its green remainder is unused clearance, not braking capability.

steps.title: Charge the complete delay
steps.description: Case 2 lengthens blind travel while keeping the drive-limit speed. The full budget still fits the rack-end line.

steps.title: Increase speed under the same delay
steps.description: Case 3 exceeds the drive limit hypothetically. Both blind travel and braking distance increase; the hatched portion crosses the fixed clearance.

title: Strain wave gear set
question: How does the disassembled gear produce a large reduction?
scope: The photograph identifies parts; it does not measure compliance, wear, or backlash.

steps.title: Impose the elliptical shape
steps.description: The wave generator bends the flexible cup into engagement at two opposite zones.

steps.title: Find the flexible output member
steps.description: The flexspline carries external teeth around its open rim and slightly fewer teeth than the circular spline.

steps.title: Count the relative advance
steps.description: The rigid ring supplies the mating internal teeth. Each generator turn advances the flexspline by the tooth-count difference, producing reduction.

title: Broken gear tooth
question: Where does a transmitted load leave visible damage?
scope: The photograph does not establish a measured stress history or the cause of this particular failure.

steps.title: Locate the interruption
steps.description: The missing tooth interrupts the repeated tooth profile; its fracture lies near the root.

steps.title: Follow the load path
steps.description: Contact forces on neighboring teeth must pass through their roots into the gear body. The root geometry concentrates bending stress.

steps.title: Separate evidence from diagnosis
steps.description: The image makes mechanical failure concrete. It cannot by itself identify the load cycles, impact, or operating command that produced it.

title: Motor stator damaged by overheating
question: Why is a motor thermal limit also an insulation limit?
scope: This opened motor illustrates components, not a temperature measurement or the running machine’s own motor.

steps.title: Locate heat generation
steps.description: Current flows through the copper windings. Resistive heating grows with current squared for a fixed effective resistance.

steps.title: Locate the vulnerable boundary
steps.description: Insulating material separates conductors and the iron core. Accumulated heat ages this insulation even when an instantaneous torque command is feasible.

steps.title: Distinguish the assembly parts
steps.description: The end bell and bearing seat support rotation; they are not the source of the winding-loss equation. A thermal qualification must concern the assembled installation.

review_notes: Inspected rendered original artwork and local QMD context; original geometry retained.

title: Torque, speed, and time on one joint motor
question: Why does a torque-speed point also need a time limit?
scope: The voltage boundary neglects winding inductance; thermal values are illustrative installation-dependent quantities.

steps.title: Check continuous feasibility
steps.description: The continuous-duty region respects rated torque and the supply-voltage boundary. Increasing speed leaves less voltage available for resistive drop.

steps.title: Treat peak torque as intermittent
steps.description: The upper region permits a burst, not indefinite operation. Back-EMF and resistive drop still impose a speed-dependent ceiling.

steps.title: Charge the initial temperature
steps.description: The same burst reaches the insulation class sooner from continuous-duty equilibrium than from ambient. A feasible instantaneous command can exhaust its thermal duration.

title: An instrumented propulsion test stand
question: What must a drive test establish beyond a data sheet?
scope: The photograph is NASA propulsion hardware, not the book’s mobile manipulator or a source of measured limits.

steps.title: Apply an actual load
steps.description: The propeller loads the electric motor. Testing an assembled propulsion system exposes conditions omitted by an isolated component rating.

steps.title: Include the electrical path
steps.description: Controller and wiring are part of the drive under test. Their limits and losses affect the operating point reached by the motor.

steps.title: Qualify stated conditions
steps.description: The stand secures and instruments the assembly. The image illustrates qualification practice; numerical ceilings require the corresponding measurements and conditions.

title: The latch corridor seen from above
question: Why do successful nominal demonstrations leave recovery unspecified?
scope: The arrows depict archive coverage and possible actions, not measured probabilities.

steps.title: Locate retained experience
steps.description: Forward actions densely populate the corridor leading to the strike plate. They describe progress from states inside that corridor.

steps.title: Move outside the archive
steps.description: The displaced gripper occupies a state with no demonstrations. Nominal forward progress does not specify an action from here.

steps.title: Identify the missing recovery
steps.description: The dashed return action is precisely the behavior missing from the archive. An unconstrained output can instead drift toward the fixture.

title: Four-stream action tap tuple
question: Which action does an imitation label actually represent?
scope: The four taps are distinct causal quantities; hardware timestamps support alignment but do not make them interchangeable.

steps.title: Record what was requested
steps.description: Tap 1 captures policy or operator intent before kinematic mapping. Tap 2 captures the mapped command instead.

steps.title: Separate proposal and permission
steps.description: Tap 3 follows the separate safety MCU’s permission path. A proposed command and an enforced command can differ.

steps.title: Observe what the plant did
steps.description: Tap 4 derives measured motion from encoders over an interval. It includes the plant response rather than merely repeating the command.

steps.title: Keep action semantics in the dataset
steps.description: All four streams meet in the telemetry log. An imitation target must name its tap and align its timestamps with the observation.

title: One lag, three verdicts
question: When does timing misalignment exceed the task clearance?
scope: Displacement equals speed times uncompensated lag here. The plotted skew range is not a separate additive allowance for every sensor.

steps.title: Convert time into position
steps.description: Each line converts lag into displacement at a stated speed. The same lag can be negligible in one task and larger than another task’s clearance.

steps.title: Test the faster approach
steps.description: The faster latch approach crosses the 2 mm clearance at 20 ms. The marked 35 ms pairing lag already exceeds that allowance.

steps.title: Check the guarded alternative
steps.description: At the guarded speed, the clearance allows 66.7 ms. This improves tolerance to lag, but does not remove the need for aligned observation and action timestamps.

title: Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop
question: Where does delay enter a leader–follower demonstration?
scope: Joint copying avoids inverse kinematics here; it does not eliminate latency or qualify permission.

steps.title: Preserve joint correspondence
steps.description: The leader and follower share joint structure, so the host can copy joint angles without solving inverse kinematics.

steps.title: Charge the forward delays
steps.description: Human response, command transfer, and mechanical response all intervene before the follower changes the scene.

steps.title: Close the human loop
steps.description: Camera transport and display delay return the scene to the operator. A recorded demonstration therefore carries the loop’s phase lag.

title: Many datasets, few episodes each
question: Does more public datasets mean long usable demonstrations?
scope: Hub creation counts include only datasets still public at retrieval; episode counts apply only to cards that report them. These are observations, not causal growth projections.

steps.title: Read the public count carefully
steps.description: The cumulative curve rises by orders of magnitude. Earlier values are lower bounds because removed or private datasets are absent.

steps.title: Inspect a different unit
steps.description: The histogram counts datasets by episodes per dataset. Its power-of-two bins show that many datasets contain only a short session.

steps.title: Separate abundance from duration
steps.description: The sparse long-session tail cannot be inferred from the cumulative dataset total. Neither panel establishes training quality or task coverage.

title: Scenario-table join for the latch
question: How can the same archive look complete and incomplete?
scope: Cell occupancy indicates available demonstrations, not evaluated competence or permission.

steps.title: Choose a narrow denominator
steps.description: The nominal table asks for one guarded-speed, nominal-offset condition. The retained archive fills that single cell.

steps.title: Ask what the task requires
steps.description: The required table adds offsets and a faster approach. The same archive fills only one of six cells.

steps.title: Count recovery without overclaiming
steps.description: The added collection fills the positive-offset guarded cell. Four cells remain known absences, and populated cells still need evaluation.

title: Covariate shift and intervention curation
question: Which takeover segments are suitable imitation targets?
scope: The plotted error and asymptotic bounds are schematic; this is a curation rule, not measured drift.

steps.title: Recognize self-induced state shift
steps.description: The policy changes the plant and thereby selects its next observations. Behavioral cloning can encounter states absent from its original demonstrations.

steps.title: Recover the lead-up to takeover
steps.description: The lookback reaches before intervention. Divergent states can be relabeled by an expert while the learner’s commands there remain masked.

steps.title: Exclude the transition
steps.description: The blend and operator reorientation are retained for diagnosis, but are not expert imitation targets.

steps.title: Begin the reviewed expert segment
steps.description: Only after measured stabilization does the reviewed recovery segment supply expert action labels.

title: What a pooled corpus actually contains
question: Does the pooled corpus match this machine’s embodiment and cadence?
scope: These are dataset-size-weighted published corpus statistics; declared command rate is not a measured control latency.

steps.title: Check embodiment composition
steps.description: Single-arm episodes dominate the morphology panel. The green mobile-manipulator bar marks the running machine’s class, not equivalent task experience.

steps.title: Compare action cadence
steps.description: The command-rate distribution concentrates at or below 10 Hz. The green 20 Hz marker identifies the running machine’s chunk renewal rate for comparison.

steps.title: Keep unknown rates unknown
steps.description: A substantial share has no declared rate, often because actions are primitive skills or quasi-static moves. Do not silently assign those episodes a compatible cadence.

title: Camera-to-robot calibration check on DROID scenes
question: What does a projected robot mask check?
scope: These DROID examples are calibration consistency evidence, not a guarantee that every pose or camera is correct.

steps.title: Compare mask to visible geometry
steps.description: The purple mask is rendered from the robot mesh at the recorded joint angles, then projected through the audited camera calibration. In this close-up, compare the mask’s joint and link boundaries with the visible arm.

steps.title: Check across viewpoints
steps.description: The bent-arm view exposes another pose and background. Agreement should persist across pose changes rather than appearing correct in only one convenient view.

steps.title: Reject inconsistent trajectories early
steps.description: Compare the projected arm and gripper in this lower-row scene. A displaced projection flags inconsistent extrinsics before training; agreement supports encoder consistency, not independent motion permission.

title: Grounded intent pipeline architecture across the silicon boundary
question: Why can grounded intent still not authorize a drive?
scope: The cost-field box is an optional producer family; the running machine emits a target pose directly. AP and MCU share no memory.

steps.title: Form a semantic proposal
steps.description: The application processor combines image, instruction, and state in its slow intent model. Its output remains a candidate.

steps.title: Reject producer ambiguity
steps.description: Only a singleton calibrated prediction set passes this producer-side gate. Passing says nothing by itself about stopping reserve or current evidence.

steps.title: Cross an explicit link
steps.description: The structured proposal crosses the board link into MCU-owned memory. It is not a shared-memory command to the drive.

steps.title: Keep admission and expiry resident
steps.description: The MCU checks evidence and physical constraints before arming its timer. Expiry stops the drives without waiting for the application processor.

title: Composing value maps for a grasp request
question: Why can a low-cost planned path still hit an obstacle?
scope: This is a schematic horizontal slice of the value-map interface, not a measured scene or a safety-qualified planner.

steps.title: Reward the named handle
steps.description: The affordance map makes locations near the requested handle attractive to the planner. It expresses the task, not all hazards.

steps.title: Penalize observed occupancy
steps.description: The avoidance map assigns cost around the observed obstacle. A missing observation contributes no such penalty.

steps.title: Trace the resulting omission
steps.description: The path avoids the mapped obstacle yet crosses the unobserved obstacle. Optimizing the composed maps cannot recover evidence that never entered them.

title: Open-vocabulary grasp grounding pipeline
question: Where does a language-conditioned grasp become only a proposal?
scope: The OK-Robot image illustrates grounding and heuristic filtering; the independent lease and permission wrapper is developed in the chapter.

steps.title: Start with observed geometry
steps.description: The robot views supply the scene, while candidate grasps cover many possible approaches.

steps.title: Use language to select the object
steps.description: The language-conditioned mask narrows the target. Object selection differs from verifying every physical consequence of a grasp.

steps.title: Filter candidate approaches
steps.description: Geometric heuristics prune the proposals. The last column shows a selected grasp candidate, not an independently admitted motion.

title: Localization uncertainty and authority expiry
question: Why do geometric uncertainty and authority expiry require separate checks?
scope: Panel a is a scaled uncertainty illustration; panel b is a schematic stop, not a measured timing trace.

steps.title: Check the limiting direction
steps.description: The lateral uncertainty fits the grasp tolerance, but depth uncertainty along the camera ray exceeds it. One fitting axis cannot validate the pose.

steps.title: Keep authority finite
steps.description: Renewals keep the lease alive. When renewals cease, the expiry timer still runs locally.

steps.title: Reserve room after expiry
steps.description: Drive onset delay and a jerk-limited stop follow expiry. Their speed–time area must fit remaining clearance; expiry does not mean instantaneous rest.

title: Mug lease against the intent model's timing
question: Can the intent producer refresh the mug target before its evidence deadline?
scope: Countdowns assume zero additional controller reserve; tracking cancels belt velocity but retains the plotted residual-slip model.

steps.title: Spend the positional tolerance
steps.description: Both error curves start with the initial error. Belt speed exhausts tolerance earlier than tracked residual slip does.

steps.title: Compare to the producer clock
steps.description: The intent inference and proposal period extend beyond both evidence horizons. Waiting for the next proposal cannot keep the target valid.

steps.title: Expire locally before a refresh
steps.description: The MCU countdowns expire at their evidence ceilings, followed by the hatched stop-onset interval. The host does not need to send a stop message.

title: Target-evidence horizon and early filters
question: Can a fresh intent arrive before its target evidence expires?
scope: The shaded region bounds target error only; it does not establish collision freedom or motion permission.

steps.title: Read the evidence deadline
steps.description: Higher residual drift shortens the time before target error uses the positional tolerance. The curve includes the initial error allowance.

steps.title: Compare with inference time
steps.description: The intent-inference reference lies above the conveyor horizon but below the slow-settling horizon. A slow producer cannot be assumed to refresh every target in time.

steps.title: Reject before expensive planning
steps.description: Sequence and evidence, workspace, transit lower bound, and ambiguity checks can reject a proposal early. Passing them leads to planning, not automatic admission.

title: Forward occupancy sets on the aisle
question: Why must a candidate corridor avoid where a person could move?
scope: The discs show only speed-bound growth. Body radius and tracking uncertainty must also enlarge the real occupancy sets.

steps.title: Anchor the prediction in evidence
steps.description: The sets are centered on the coworker’s last measured position. They bound possible occupancy rather than predict one chosen walking direction.

steps.title: Charge the longer horizon
steps.description: The tracked evidence horizon gives a larger growth set. The red corridor segment enters that set and must be refused.

steps.title: Account for the full envelope
steps.description: At the long horizon the growth spans the aisle. The drawn discs still omit body radius and tracking terms, so they are not complete clearance envelopes.

title: Intent lease lifecycle
question: Which event is allowed to renew authority?
scope: The lifecycle is a guarded state machine; elapsed visual playback is not a real lease clock.

steps.title: Start with no authority
steps.description: Pending proposals either pass admission and arm a timer or are refused with no authority.

steps.title: Demand a genuinely fresh renewal
steps.description: Active and Renewed hold the lease. A higher sequence, newer capture, and passing permission check are required; a stale renewal cannot reset the timer.

steps.title: Distinguish completion from failure
steps.description: Terminal predicates can complete the goal. Timer expiry, contact limits, or evidence loss instead end the held lease.

steps.title: Select a validated fallback
steps.description: Expiry and abort start the fallback chosen by the MCU for the measured state. They do not wait for another intent proposal.

title: A decade of reported takeovers
question: What can reported disengagement statistics actually compare?
scope: These are one company’s annual testing-permit filings. Reportability definitions vary and commercial deployment miles are excluded.

steps.title: Establish exposure and permit
steps.description: The stacked bars distinguish safety-driver testing from driverless testing. Their sum concerns testing exposure, not all commercial operation.

steps.title: Read the denominator
steps.description: Miles per reported disengagement divides the corresponding miles by reported events. A larger value is not a direct guarantee of physical safety.

steps.title: Preserve reporting scope
steps.description: The driverless series covers different years and permit exposure. Neither this within-company plot nor its reporting rules support an uncontrolled comparison across companies.

title: Where an in-loop takeover spends its time
question: Which takeover stage first uses up the spare clearance?
scope: Human-processor intervals are conservative model allocations, not measured guarantees. Local commit precedes commit notification.

steps.title: Spend clearance before the person reacts
steps.description: Video transport alone consumes the machine’s spare distance at the stated aisle speed. A remote operator has not yet completed perception.

steps.title: Include the complete human response
steps.description: Perception, decision, and motor response follow. They are sequential budget allocations rather than an instantaneous human safety layer.

steps.title: Separate commit from notification
steps.description: The handshake ends at notification, while local commit already starts the enforcer-owned blend. The full exchange remains the conservative waiting allocation.

title: Two takeovers against one clear distance
question: Why does waiting for takeover change the stop even with identical brakes?
scope: All traces use the same resident jerk-limited stop after their respective delays; takeover does not improve braking.

steps.title: Read the resident margin
steps.description: The machine-only trace stops below the clear-distance line. Its spare is the budget available before added waiting becomes a breach.

steps.title: Insert in-loop waiting
steps.description: The in-loop trace coasts longer before the same braking profile. It crosses the clearance line despite unchanged brakes.

steps.title: Extend the view for out-of-loop delay
steps.description: The lower panel shows the full out-of-loop takeover. Much of its travel occurs before any brake command; waiting, rather than weaker deceleration, spends the clearance.

title: Industrial teach pendant with three-position enabling grip
question: Which safety controls can this front view actually show?
scope: The rear three-position enabling grip and safety wiring are not visible. The photograph establishes no device timing.

steps.title: Separate interface from protective input
steps.description: The display presents the operator interface. The red mushroom is the visible emergency-stop actuator.

steps.title: Locate manual command input

steps.title: Respect what is out of view
steps.description: The attached cable is visible, but the rear enabling grip and its safety circuit are not. Do not infer their position or wiring from this front view.

title: Authority states and their guards
question: When does authority move from policy to operator?
scope: The enforcer owns the blend. Human manual proposals require completed transfer and a live lease; protection preempts all enclosed states.

steps.title: Request without transferring authority
steps.description: The pending state leaves the policy proposing while its timer runs. A request alone does not enable manual control.

steps.title: Commit on a control tick
steps.description: Acknowledgment and commit start the blend. The enforcer, rather than a live operator stream, owns the latched profile.

steps.title: Require the live manual lease
steps.description: Only completion of the profile with a valid manual lease permits human-manual proposals. Lease lapse or invalid state instead reaches fallback.

steps.title: Keep protective preemption independent
steps.description: The hardwired protective input can preempt every enclosed state. Resetting fallback requires rest and fresh re-admission.

title: Step vs. quintic command transfer
question: What does a quintic blend bound compared with an ideal step?
scope: The gray ringing is illustrative. Command derivative is not measured actuator jerk, and bounded rate alone does not prove stability.

steps.title: Identify the instantaneous demand
steps.description: The step changes command at once; its ideal derivative is an impulse. That ideal demand is distinct from a physical actuator response.

steps.title: Do not read a measured response
steps.description: The gray ringing is schematic. It illustrates a concern without reporting a tested plant trace.

steps.title: Spread the transfer in time
steps.description: The fixed-endpoint quintic changes command over the blend window with a bounded derivative. The bound concerns commanded rate under these endpoints.

review_notes: Inspected rendered original artwork and local QMD context; original geometry retained.

title: Six decisions behind one admitted command
question: Which decisions cannot be recovered from a runtime log alone?
scope: The arrows trace responsibility, not a sequential runtime execution path.

steps.title: Start at the admitted command
steps.description: A single admitted tick depends on decisions made by different parties before execution. A correct enforcement log does not identify every owner.

steps.title: Trace the existing records
steps.description: Policy weights, enforcer thresholds, authority state, and operating envelope have named records. These records expose four decision links.

steps.title: Find the unrecorded premises
steps.description: Facility crossing rules and operations staffing ratios have no record in this chain. Runtime telemetry cannot manufacture their ownership.

steps.title: Bind decisions to owners
steps.description: The approval record collects each decision and its owner. An ownerless link requires refusal rather than treating missing accountability as harmless paperwork.

title: One stop, two groups of people
question: How does later detection turn the same stop into contact?
scope: The model assumes independent detection frames, fixed speed and braking, and a stop sized to the reference group. Recall disparity alone does not determine impact.

steps.title: Hold the initial speed fixed
steps.description: Both groups begin at the same machine speed. The lower-detection group requires additional frames before braking begins.

steps.title: Keep braking capability unchanged
steps.description: The delayed curve follows the same deceleration law, shifted later in distance. The reference stop reaches rest just before the person.

steps.title: Read the physical consequence
steps.description: At the person line the delayed curve still has speed, producing the labeled impact energy under the chapter’s mass and braking assumptions. The lost distance connects detection delay to harm.
